# Phase 13 — the paired machine control

<!-- Generated by hand from `benchmarks/external/PAIRED_CONTROL.md`. Numbers only, no source text. -->

```text
license/provenance status: unclear for dialogue data
local evaluation exception; not redistributable by this project
```

## The question this phase had to answer

Every measurement before it compared **one corpus against another**: V2EX forum replies
against a generated benchmark, LCCC human dialogue against generated text. A rule that
fires more often on one than the other can be explained by the topic, the register, the
context length, the reply length or the data source — all of them at once, and none of
them separable. So the question that decides which rules deserve to exist was open:

> Which rules actually measure machine-shaped **chat behaviour**, rather than some
> artefact of text length, punctuation habit, forum register or data source?

## The design

One LCCC context, continued four times. Same topic, same register, same length pressure;
the only thing that differs is who wrote the next line.

| Arm | What produced it |
| --- | --- |
| `human` | the LCCC continuation, unchanged — the control |
| `plain` | a model answering the conversation with no constraints |
| `default` | a model answering under this suite's own chat contract, quoted from `human_voice_prepare` rather than paraphrased |
| `post` | the `plain` answer rewritten under the same contract — the suite's real pipeline shape |

Three machine conditions rather than one bucket, because "a model wrote this" and "this
behaves like an assistant" are different claims and only the second is this project's.

Items were drawn **round-robin across 59 strata cells** — single/multi-turn, user-input
length, context length, human-reply length, turn type — so no stratum can masquerade as
the sample. 2,000 items, 6,000 machine continuations, nothing missing, nothing refused.

## What was built

| File | What it is for |
| --- | --- |
| `benchmarks/external/paired-sample.ts` | draws the stratified items from LCCC's held-out splits, and writes the committable census |
| `benchmarks/external/paired-generate.ts` | writes the chunk files that carry the brief, then merges and validates what came back |
| `benchmarks/external/paired-report.ts` | measures all four arms and writes `PAIRED_CONTROL.md` |
| `benchmarks/external/selection.ts` | the round-robin draw |
| `benchmarks/external/reply-rules.ts` | what counts as a reply, and what counts as a refusal |
| `benchmarks/external/conditions.ts`, `labels.ts` | the condition list and the two mandatory labels, in modules that do not run a tool when imported |

Generation is performed by the harness's own agents: there is **no model inside this
suite**, by design, so the experiment uses the one it is installed into. Each unit of
work is a chunk file carrying its condition's brief verbatim, which is what keeps two
generators from differing in anything but the context they were handed.

## Six defects in the experiment's own tooling

Recorded because each one would have produced a confident, wrong number.

1. **The "stratified" sample was one stratum.** The balanced view is written cell by
   cell, so `slice(0, 120)` took 120 items of the first cell. The first run reported a
   user-input-length table with a single row, `long`, which is what gave it away.
   Fixed by `selectStratified`: one item from every cell, then a second from every cell.
2. **Every rate was half what it should have been.** A continuation is scanned twice —
   once for the behaviour family, once for the prose families — and the first version
   counted both passes in the denominator. 240 "pairs" from 120 items.
3. **Reused answers were destroyed by a file-name collision.** Chunk output files were
   named by chunk number, so a new selection overwrote the previous run's answers with
   different items while the incremental logic still counted them as done. Output names
   now carry the first item id.
4. **A ratio against zero was printed as a ratio.** `16666666.7×` more often on machine
   continuations, from dividing by `1e-9`. Now printed as `6 firing(s) against 0`.
5. **A real chat reply was dropped as a refusal.** The refusal pattern began with a bare
   `抱歉`, so any reply opening with an apology was discarded — and an apology followed
   by an explanation for being late is one of the most ordinary messages in Chinese
   chat. The one row this cost is quoted nowhere here, because it is LCCC-derived text:
   the fix is that an apology now counts as a refusal only when the refusal follows it,
   and `tests/paired-reply-rules.test.ts` pins both directions.
6. **Importing the condition list ran the generator's command line** — twice, in two
   different files. The definitions now live in modules whose import has no side effect,
   which is also what made the refusal rule testable.

## What it found

**Three rules separate machine chat from human chat, and they separate cleanly.** Each
fires on machine continuations and on **none of the 2,000 human ones**:

| Rule | `plain` | `default` | `post` | `human` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `chat.unsolicited_advice` | 32 (1.6%) | 14 (0.7%) | 22 (1.1%) | **0** |
| `chat.forced_positivity` | 33 (1.7%) | 8 (0.4%) | 22 (1.1%) | **0** |
| `chat.over_agreement` | 26 (1.3%) | 11 (0.5%) | 25 (1.3%) | **0** |

Six more rules fired too rarely to classify: `chat.mirrors_user`, `chat.explains_obvious`,
`assistant.chatbot_residue`, `lexical.aphorism_dressing` and
`lexical.translationese_connective` on machine text and never on human text, plus
`rhythm.repeated_openings` once, on the human side.

**Between them the three catch 89 of 2,000 `plain` continuations (4.5%), 32 `default`
(1.6%), 67 `post` (3.4%) and 0 human.** That is the recall of the behaviour layer on
machine chat in this register, and it belongs beside the precision: a rule that never
fires on human writing and catches one machine continuation in twenty is a rule that
finds a real thing rarely.

**The firings are structure, not noise.** 123 items (6.2%) were caught in at least one
machine condition, and **72 of those were caught by two or three conditions** against
6.5 expected if the conditions fired independently. `chat.unsolicited_advice` fired on
four of the same items under both `plain` and `default` against 0.22 expected;
`chat.forced_positivity` on four against 0.13. The rules are reading something about the
continuation rather than sampling it at random — which is also what makes the 1% rates
worth reading as rates.

**The prose families say nothing at all in this register.** `antiAIScore` was `1.000` for
all four arms: 8,000 texts of chat length produced no structural, lexical, rhythm,
Chinese, English or stylometry finding of any consequence. That is a statement about the
domain the prose rules were built for, not about whether they work — and it means that
for chat-length input, the behaviour family is the only part of the suite that speaks.

**The behaviour layer is a low-recall one.** `ASSISTANT_SHAPED` was crossed by 0 of 2,000
human continuations, 2 of 2,000 `plain`, 1 of 2,000 `default` and 2 of 2,000 `post`; mean
`behaviorScore` was 0.994, 0.993, 0.997 and 0.994. Even a completely unconstrained model
is caught on roughly one turn in a thousand by the layer as a whole.

**The contract works, and what it does is shorten.** Taken together the three separating
rules fire 91 times under `plain`, **33** under `default` and 69 under `post`: generating
under the contract removes about two thirds of them, rewriting afterwards about a
quarter. Mean reply length moves 20.3 → **12.3** characters, against 38.1 for the human
control, so part of that improvement is brevity. Related: **the `post` arm is the same
text as `plain` in 1,158 of 2,000 items (57.9%)** — for replies this short the rewrite
step frequently finds nothing to change, which is why its numbers track `plain`'s.

**The rates hold when the sample is re-weighted to LCCC's own mix.** The measured view is
balanced by construction, so each cell contributes about the same, which is not how LCCC
looks. Post-stratifying each cell's measured rate by its share of the natural draw — no
extra generation needed — moves the three separating rules by at most 0.5 points
(`chat.forced_positivity` 1.7% → 2.0% under `plain`, 0.4% → 0.7% under `default`) and
leaves them machine-only. It moves `chat.over_completeness` a long way: 3.0% → **1.0%**,
because the long, many-sentence replies it needs are over-represented in a balanced view
and rare in the corpus. All three figures are in `PAIRED_CONTROL.md` §8.

## Class A, and why nothing was changed

`chat.over_completeness` fired on **60 of 2,000** human continuations (3.0% balanced,
**1.0%** weighted to LCCC's own distribution) and on **0** of the 6,000 machine ones. Read
alone that is a direction defect — a rule firing on human chat and never on machine chat.

It is not that. The rule needs a reply of more than four sentences, and the report's shape
check is decisive: **87 of 2,000 human continuations reached five sentences; all three
machine arms reached it 0 times.** The machine arms could not trigger the rule, so their
zero is not evidence that the rule is safe — it is evidence that this register gives the
rule no chance. The part that *was* measured is the human side, 3.0% balanced and 1.0%
re-weighted, and that is a false-positive rate.

So the rule stays as it is, which is also what the repository owner instructed before the
experiment ran. `benchmarks/external/README.md` now carries it in the hypothesis ledger as
**open, not reproduced**, which is what stops it being quietly forgotten or quietly
"fixed".

## What this phase did not do

- **No rule was changed.** Not one of the thirteen rule changes in
  `docs/phase-8-rule-changes.md` came from here, and nothing in `benchmarks/corpora/`
  moved: the committed corpus still measures 3.52 tells per 1,000 characters.
- **No scale beyond 2,000 items.** 10,000, 30,000 and the full 55,925 pairs are the
  owner's decision, to be taken on these results rather than before them.
- **No second generator.** Each arm is one model at one setting, so each is a point and
  not a distribution. The comparison is between conditions, not between models.

## The instrument this leaves behind

`benchmarks/external/README.md` now states the procedure a corpus finding has to pass —
propose, reproduce on shippable text, measure against the committed corpus, then change
and record — with a ledger naming what is landed and what is open. This phase is the
first one to produce an open entry rather than a fix, and that is the honest outcome: the
experiment can say which three rules are doing the work, and it can say that the fourth
question cannot be settled in this register.
